title: Semantic Routing and Authority-Weighted Retrieval for Technical Infrastructure RAG: A Phase 4 Companion Study
abstract: The base study established that nomic-embed-text outperforms largerdense and hybrid embedding models on a technical infrastructure RAGcorpus, and named three Phase 4 extensions as future work: a semanticrouter using a lightweight classifier language model, anauthority-weighted corpus prioritizing live device state over staticdesign documentation, and a full-corpus re-benchmark against theoriginal 30-question evaluation set. This companion study reports theresults of implementing and empirically testing all three. Theproposed 0.6B-parameter router classifier measured 33% four-wayclassification accuracy — far below the near-perfect classificationthe base study's projected 88% combined accuracy assumed — and wasreplaced with a deterministic rule-based classifier that measured 100%on the same evaluation set. The resulting router did not outperform asingle well-chosen model and retrieval backend on either the originalbenchmark or a new 15-question set targeting freshly-ingested content.Authority weighting produced a consistent, twice-replicated improvementon stale-versus-fresh factual disambiguation, but a corroboratedfailure mode on multi-step reasoning questions. Neither of the basestudy's two named authority-weighting target questions was resolved bythe proposed mechanism itself. The live-state pull separately surfacedand — under one specific retrieval configuration — resolved a corpusdefect that had persisted, undetected, through three prior researchphases. A controlled measurement found generation-time samplingvariance of up to 6 combined percentage points, a larger noise bandthan previously reported.

title: A world model as a judge: early, auditable verdicts on partial robot-manipulation rollouts.
abstract: We present LeWorldModel Judge, a locked benchmark and an auditable judging surface for scoring partial robot-manipulation rollouts before their episodes end. Sparse terminal reward answers no useful question about a trajectory prefix: whether the rollout is still on track, already doomed, or physically implausible only becomes visible in hindsight, which makes early triage, data curation, and process-reward experiments needlessly blind. We lock a narrow evaluation slice (three Meta-World tasks, four constructed policy families, prefix cutoffs at 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75 of the horizon), define heuristic but fully inspectable prefix labels, and score every prefix with a cutoff-time composite judge over named evidence signals, alongside a replay-time latent proxy whose causal limitation we state exactly. A mandatory calibration protocol reports the provenance of every decision threshold and only grants held-out status when the calibration and evaluation policy families are disjoint. On a fresh 90-prefix held-out slice collected after the label rules were frozen, the composite judge reaches a 0.949 failure hit rate at a 0.137 false positive rate and 0.978 pairwise ranking accuracy, against 0.50 and 0.554 for sparse-reward and progress baselines, and the threshold calibrated on disjoint families transfers across disjoint captures to within 0.0004 (0.2977 versus 0.2980). Every reported number decomposes to named sub-scores in checked-in files, carries a judge_mode provenance tag, and regenerates from a pinned command line.

title: Intermediate-Task Diversity and Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer Performance
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: How does the choice of intermediate-task diversity (e.g., task type, domain) affect zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on XTREME-R and XQuAD, as measured by accuracy and F1 scores? title: Solving the Challenge of Protein Folding with Quantum Computing... Demonstration of a Resource-Efficient Quantum Algorithm
abstract: - A study published in the international journal npj Quantum Information (Nature Portfolio) presents a resource-efficient quantum algorithm framework based on the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) for peptide and protein folding. - By translating protein folding into a tetrahedral lattice model and combining Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) VQE with a classical evolutionary algorithm, the number of required qubits was drastically reduced. - It successfully folded a 7-amino acid neuropeptide using only 9 qubits on actual IBM 20-qubit quantum hardware, demonstrating its practical potential for next-generation drug discovery in the NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) era. [Quantum Biology Society] The protein folding problem, which involves predicting the three-dimensional structure of proteins and peptides from their primary amino acid sequence, plays a central role in various applications such as chemistry, biology, and medicine. However, as the sequence lengthens, the number of possible structures to explore explodes exponentially, making it difficult for classical computers to handle its intrinsic NP-hard complexity. Recently, a new quantum algorithm that can efficiently solve this long-standing challenge even on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) computers has been developed, drawing the attention of the academic community. The paper titled "Resource-efficient quantum algorithm for protein folding," published in the international journal npj Quantum Information, presents an innovative computing framework for the discovery of next-generation peptide drugs. The research team of Anton Robert and Ivano Tavernelli from IBM Quantum, IBM Research - Zurich in Switzerland successfully led this groundbreaking study. ■ The Meeting of Lattice Models and Qubit Optimization Until now, attempts to introduce quantum computing to protein folding have required an unattainably high number of qubits that current, near-term quantum hardware cannot handle. To solve this, the research team converted protein folding into a tetrahedral lattice model. This model can efficiently depict the growth of a polymer chain while maintaining chemically plausible bond angles. In particular, they adopted a method of adding penalty terms to the Hamiltonian to prevent unphysical amino acid overlaps (e.g., beads occupying the same lattice site). Through this, they succeeded in drastically reducing the number of qubits required for calculation while suppressing the complexity of the algorithm to the level of O(N⁴). ■ Demonstration of Folding on Actual Quantum Hardware This algorithm maximized efficiency by combining CVaR-VQE, a variation of the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), with a classical Differential Evolution optimizer. Applying this technique, the researchers simulated the folding of the 10-amino acid Angiotensin peptide using only 22 qubits, successfully finding the most stable energy state (native fold). Furthermore, they successfully demonstrated the folding of a 7-amino acid neuropeptide (APRLRFY) using only 9 qubits on IBM's 20-qubit quantum computer hardware. This study is a groundbreaking achievement proving that the protein folding problem, which previously required massive computing resources, can be successfully solved even in a noisy real quantum processor environment. It is expected to bring tremendous innovation to next-generation /de novo/ drug design and disease treatment research utilizing quantum computing in the future.

title: Promoting Diversity in Cartesian Genetic Programming for Image Processing with Equality Graphs
abstract: Cartesian Genetic Programming (CGP) constrains the search space of programs stimulating modularity, leading to smaller programs. This constraint is innate of its representation as each program is represented as a sequence of instructions and each instruction can only be applied to the output of one of the previously generated instructions, effectively reducing the search space. However, the search is biased by the initial solutions and the existence of a neutral space, slowing down the exploration. Recently, a new method for improving the exploration in genetic programming (GP) was proposed with the use of equality graphs (e-graphs), an efficient data structure that stores the visitation history of the search which can be exploited to create novel solutions. This algorithm was successful in improving the exploration while achieving a state-of-the-art performance in symbolic regression. In this paper, we apply the same idea for CGP to enforce the generation of novel solutions. We also exploit this information to detect when the search stagnates, prompting a restart with a random solution. The results on image processing tasks showed improvements over CGP reinforcing the need for better diversity inducing mechanisms in GP.

title: Conditional Independence Testing with Tuning: An Approach Based on Predictive Performance
abstract: Abstract Conditional independence testing is fundamental in predictive and causal modeling. While numerous tests have been proposed in the literature, many suffer from limitations such as strong parametric assumptions, restrictions on variable types, or prohibitive computational cost—making them ill-suited for application to complex, real-world datasets. Recent non-parametric approaches address these issues by testing conditional independence based on predictive performance. The core idea is that if two variables X and Y are conditionally dependent given a set Z, then a predictive model using both X and Z to predict Y should outperform a model that uses only Z. Building on this principle, we propose a non-parametric conditional independence test that leverages the capabilities of Automated Machine Learning (AutoML). We design an architecture that not only selects and tunes predictive models, but also ensures the statistical robustness of the test. Unlike previous methods, our approach maintains proper test calibration (Type I error control) and power, and minimizes computational cost. In addition, it is robust to different data types (including mixed data), functional relationships, and large sample sizes or conditioning sets. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate the practical applicability of our method and its competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art alternatives.

title: An efficient algorithm for approximate shadow Hamiltonian simulation
abstract: We propose an efficient algorithm based on shadow Hamiltonian simulation to approximately simulate the real-time dynamics of observables under time-independent Hamiltonians. Shadow Hamiltonian simulation works at the level of the operator algebra generated by the observables through commutators with the Hamiltonian. Exactly encoding the quantum state in this picture is generally inefficient for interacting systems due to the exponential growth of the operator algebra. Our algorithm overcomes this bottleneck by systematically identifying the elements of the algebra most relevant to the target observables. This targeted approach is a controlled approximation that yields a highly efficient quantum state encoding that substantially reduces the size of the qubit register required to perform the time evolution using the shadow Hamiltonian. We propose two main pruning schemes, one based on a predefined operator basis and another on a constructed Krylov basis. We also present a hybrid scheme that builds a Krylov basis within a pruned algebra in the predefined basis. We benchmark our algorithm using lattice spin systems in one and two dimensions, for both one- and higher-point correlators as observables.

title: A Glimpse into Long-term Physical Coexistence with Intelligent Robots
abstract: Long-term physical coexistence with intelligent robots requires more than capable robot policies. A persistent robotic assistant must support diverse user-facing interfaces, maintain long-horizon memory of people and preferences, coordinate across robot embodiments, and translate human intent into safe physical execution. We introduce PHILIA, a multi-robot agent built around a robot gateway abstraction. PHILIA retains the rich interaction and tool ecosystem of OpenClaw while exposing robot-local runtimes, onboard perception, navigation, speaker, and robot policies through a unified capability interface. This design decouples low-frequency, high-semantic agent reasoning from high-frequency, low-level robot execution, enabling plug-and-play integration of user interfaces, robot embodiments, and policy backends. As a result, the user experience becomes compositional: advances in user interfaces, robot embodiments, robot policies, navigation, or interaction algorithms can improve the overall experience without redesigning the system. We validate the architecture on Astribot S1 robots while designing the robot gateway contract to support future heterogeneous robot platforms through a shared capability interface for observation, task execution, navigation, speech playback, status monitoring, and task cancellation. We present representative use cases in which agent memory and scene understanding are grounded in robot actions. These span interactive household scenarios, ranging from simple organization to challenging long-horizon and dexterous service tasks, such as packing a backpack and lifting a garbage bag. We highlight the human-robot interaction flow, where contextual understanding of user intent and preferences, together with human-in-the-loop confirmation or adjustment during execution, is essential for effective assistance.

title: SARG-QLoRA: Syntax-Aware Retrieval-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Dependency Parsing with Autoregressive Large Language Models
abstract: Reference implementation and reproducibility artefacts accompanying the paper "SARG-QLoRA: Syntax-Aware Retrieval-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Dependency Parsing with Autoregressive Large Language Models." SARG-QLoRA couples Syntax-Aware Retrieval Guidance (SARG) -- a retrieval mechanism that selects supporting exemplars by structural similarity rather than semantic similarity -- with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) fine-tuning of a 3B-parameter instruction-tuned backbone, to perform generative dependency parsing on a single commodity GPU. Output reliability is validated with a four-criterion Tree Validity Checker (TVC), applied independently of gold-reference annotations. Trained and evaluated on the Universal Dependencies English Web Treebank, the model achieves 81.35% UAS / 78.28% LAS (within 1.07 points of the specialist Stanza parser while updating only 0.75% of model parameters), 96.97% structural validity under the Tree Validity Checker, and sustains zero-shot cross-lingual transfer to Spanish, German, and French without any multilingual training data. This archive includes the paper source (LaTeX), the full experiment notebook, real model prediction outputs, result tables, and a standalone, independently-runnable script (tvc_scoring.py) that recomputes every structural-reliability figure reported in the paper directly from the model's own saved output.

SARG-QLoRA couples Syntax-Aware Retrieval Guidance (SARG) -- a retrieval mechanism that selects supporting exemplars by structural similarity rather than semantic similarity -- with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) fine-tuning of a 3B-parameter instruction-tuned backbone, to perform generative dependency parsing on a single commodity GPU. Output reliability is validated with a four-criterion Tree Validity Checker (TVC), applied independently of gold-reference annotations. Trained and evaluated on the Universal Dependencies English Web Treebank, the model achieves 81.35% UAS / 78.28% LAS (within 1.07 points of the specialist Stanza parser while updating only 0.75% of model parameters), 96.97% structural validity under the Tree Validity Checker, and sustains zero-shot cross-lingual transfer to Spanish, German, and French without any multilingual training data. This archive includes the paper source (LaTeX), the full experiment notebook, real model prediction outputs, result tables, and a standalone, independently-runnable script (tvc_scoring.py) that recomputes every structural-reliability figure reported in the paper directly from the model's own saved output.
